news.title: Green-led council plans to ban cooperation with Home Office on immigration raids
news.summary:
Exclusive: Lewisham council’s move marks first step in Greens’ plan to create a corridor of sanctuary boroughs across London

A Green-led London council is planning to ban its officials from working with the Home Office on immigration raids, after uncovering evidence suggesting government officials wanted to use environmental health data to target restaurant workers.

Councillors on the Lewisham borough council are due to vote next week on a motion that would review its systems with a view to ending any cooperation with the government’s attempts to deport people without the right

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham forecasts £10.0m high needs overspend for 2026/27 as children with EHCPs rise to 4,032
news_drafts.lead:
Lewisham Council is forecasting a £10.0m overspend in 2026/27 on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Its period 6 monitoring report to the Public Accounts Select Committee says "there are now 4,032 children with an EHCP", an education, health and care plan. That is 231 more than the 3,801 in September 2025.

The paper gives average placement costs of £15k a year for children placed in the borough and £27k for those placed outside it. The council's cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, stood at £24.4m at 31 March 2026. The statutory override, a government rule that lets councils keep such a deficit off their main balance sheet, "has been extended to 31st March 2028".

Table 11 of the report shows a deficit of £34.0m at the end of 2026/27, and £34.4m for the high needs block. The paper does not reconcile the two figures. The Department for Education (DfE) notified the council on 5 October 2026 that "the DfE has deferred the decision on the SEND Reform Plan". The council must resubmit the plan by the end of November 2026, with a decision expected in January 2027. The paper says the plan could bring grant of up to 90% of eligible expenditure, and that it is unclear what support will be given for the remaining deficit.

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham forecasts £9.9m gross overspend for 2026/27, £7.0m after mitigations, with £9.7m of savings undelivered
news_drafts.lead:
Lewisham Council is forecasting a gross overspend of £9.9m on its 2026/27 outturn, according to papers for the Children and Young People Select Committee on 11 November. After mitigations, the net overspend for the year is £7.0m.

The figures come from the council's monitoring at period 4, presented to the Mayor and Cabinet in October 2026. The paper says that within the overspend there is "£9.7m of savings not being delivered". The Children and Young People savings report says the council continues to monitor and forecast its outturn. It gives the gross figure without setting out how the overspend will be funded.

The monitoring paper says officers are working to identify which part of the 2026/27 overspend will persist into 2027/28. The papers give no breakdown of the overspend by service and no figure for that part.

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham's 2027/28 budget report to assume up to £30m of reserves for any savings shortfall
news_drafts.lead:
Lewisham Council's 2027/28 budget report will be written on the basis that up to £30m of reserves will be needed to cover any savings shortfall. That is set out in a savings report before the Safer Stronger Communities Select Committee, which meets on 10 November 2026. The report's appendix calls this a fallback position pending agreement of further proposals.

The cover report says the proposals put forward so far do not meet the budget gap. Officers will continue to work up new proposals totalling at least £20m, to be developed as part of setting the 2027/28 budget. The report gives the aim as minimising the risk of needing reserves to set a balanced budget next year.

The appendix also covers what happens to any shortfall. If proposals totalling £30m cannot be identified or agreed, it says, the difference falls to reserves for 2027/28 and "will immediately be added to the 2028/29 savings target which is already £13.985m." It adds that the 2027/28 budget will be set using reserves to the extent of any shortfall as a minimum.

findings.paper_title: 6. Period 6 Monitoring Report Draft - PASC Copy
findings.headline: The Period 6 report does not yet include transitional costs of the new administration
findings.detail: The paper says one-off transition costs are assumed to be funded from corporate provisions, and that any new priorities which cannot be accommodated within the budget will be reported as an overspend. The corporate strategy that the 2026/27 budget was set against ran 2022 to 2026.
findings.matters: A change of administration that is yet to be costed means the forecast could change once transition costs are included, which other councils going through a similar change would want to plan for.
findings.quote: This reporting does not yet include any transitional costs

findings.paper_title: 6. Period 6 Monitoring Report Draft - PASC Copy
findings.headline: CPI is 3.5% in September 2026 against 3.0% budgeted for 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper says CPI has risen from 1.7% in September 2024 and was 3.1% in August 2026. It says the rate affects council contracts and drives the inflation requests from social care providers.
findings.matters: Inflation running above the budgeted rate feeds directly into contract and social care costs, and the gap is the kind of assumption other councils would want to test.
findings.figures: 3.5% CPI in September 2026; 3.1% in August 2026; 3.0% budgeted; 1.7% low in September 2024

findings.paper_title: 6. Period 6 Monitoring Report Draft - PASC Copy
findings.headline: Schools in deficit fell to 24 at the end of 2025/26, from 25 at the end of 2024/25
findings.detail: The number of schools in deficit has risen from 13 at the end of 2021/22 to a peak of 25, and has now fallen to 24. The paper does not give the cause of the fall.
findings.matters: A fall in the number of schools in deficit is a sign that school-level budget management is improving, which other councils with deficit schools may wish to compare.
findings.figures: 24 schools in deficit at end of 2025/26; 25 at end of 2024/25; 13 at end of 2021/22
findings.quote: has reduced to 24 at the end of 2025/26

findings.paper_title: 6. Period 6 Monitoring Report Draft - PASC Copy
findings.headline: DfE has deferred its decision on Lewisham's SEND Reform Plan, with resubmission due by end of November 2026
findings.detail: The DfE notified the council on 5 October 2026 that the plan must be resubmitted by the end of November 2026, with a decision expected in January 2027. The paper says it is not yet clear how much support will be provided.
findings.matters: Whether the council receives grant support for its high-needs deficit depends on a decision not expected until January 2027, which affects planning for other councils in similar positions.
findings.figures: Resubmission by end of November 2026; decision expected January 2027
findings.quote: the DfE has deferred the decision on the SEND Reform Plan

findings.paper_title: 6. Period 6 Monitoring Report Draft - PASC Copy
findings.headline: DSG deficit stood at £24.4m at 31 March 2026, and the statutory override has been extended to 31 March 2028
findings.detail: Table 11 shows an end-2026/27 deficit of £34.0m, with £34.4m shown for the High Needs Block, and the paper does not reconcile these two figures. The paper says the SEND Reform Plan could bring grant of up to 90% of eligible expenditure, but it is unclear what support will be given for the remaining deficit.
findings.matters: A cumulative DSG deficit covered by a statutory override that now runs to 2028 is a balance-sheet exposure that other councils and lenders would track closely.

daily_post.headline: Lewisham says its revised MTFS will follow the Autumn Budget Statement on 28 October 2026 and be published with the 2027/28 Budget Report
daily_post.lead: A revised MTFS will reset the savings target and the reliance on reserves, so the timing and content will be the next point at which the council's position can be compared with peers.
